explanations: terra: The command فَٱتَّقُوا ٱلنَّارَ tells hearers to guard against the Fire, setting active caution beside the promise that the most cautious will be kept from it.

luna: The section's untrained camel resists being ridden, while the cow in 2:71 is explicitly not subdued for plowing or irrigation. Its different work setting marks the boundary between a tractable mount and an animal not yet made useful for labor. | terra: The required cow is لَا ذَلُولٌ, not trained to work the earth or water the field, a Qur'anic boundary case for an animal not broken to human direction.
terra: Hearts become harder than stone even though stones split, release water, or fall in fear of God; this resistant hardness reverses the section's softened human-animal response.
terra: Ships that run through the sea with what benefits people are among God's signs, another useful conveyance sustained within His ordering.

luna: The source-section roots ي س ر and ع س ر describe the easy-following mount against the untrained camel. In 2:185, ease and difficulty are explicitly contrasted in God's instruction about fasting, repeating that lexical opposition in a different obligation. | terra: God desires yusr for people and does not desire ʿusr, explicitly setting the section's easy and resistant conditions against each other.
terra: Pilgrims are told to take provision, while the best provision is taqwa; caution becomes equipment for an actual journey.
terra: The prayer وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ asks God to do the protecting from fire, matching the section's insistence on protection received rather than self-achieved.
terra: In danger believers may pray on foot or mounted and must remember God when secure, joining riding, fear, safety, and commanded remembrance.
terra: God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity, a moral analogue to tack that bears without injuring the back.
terra: The faithful pray وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, another direct request that the Lord supply protection from fire.
terra: The people stood at the brink of a pit of fire and God rescued them from it, combining dangerous footing, imminent fall, and deliverance by another.
terra: وَٱتَّقُوا ٱلنَّارَ commands guarding against a prepared fire; 92:17 completes the boundary by assigning actual removal to God.

luna: The section makes being kept away from the Fire the outcome of the guided, God-fearing person. 3:185 defines success as being moved far from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, spelling out what this avoidance means. | terra: Success is defined as being moved away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, turning rescue into a spatial removal performed upon the person.
terra: Contemplative believers end their prayer with فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, assigning the decisive guarding to God.
terra: Avoiding the major forbidden acts brings expiation and an honorable entrance, extending the ج ن ب family's deliberate separation from danger.

luna: The source-section dictionary phrase جنبت الدابة means leading an animal to one's side. 4:36 uses الْجَارِ الْجُنُبِ for the neighbor at one's side, a different sense of the same root that makes the side relation social rather than equestrian.
terra: Believers are commanded فَٱجْتَنِبُوهُ concerning intoxicants, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows; the same root makes avoidance an enacted separation from idolatrous practice.
terra: Whoever has punishment diverted from him on that Day has received God's mercy, a direct nonlexical counterpart to being made to pass away from fire.
terra: Those who deny the meeting with God carry their burdens upon their backs, reversing the beneficial bearer into a person crushed by his own load.
terra: Some livestock are burden-bearers and some close to the ground, a bodily classification that foregrounds animals fitted to human use.
terra: No bearer of burdens bears another's moral burden, a boundary against transferring the load even though a mount physically carries its rider.
terra: The people of the Garden are introduced with the assurance that no soul is charged beyond its capacity, a boundary on burdens placed upon the traveler.

luna: The section says the saved person cannot pull himself away from the Fire; another holds the reins. In 7:43 the people of the Garden say they would not have been guided unless God had guided them, directly expressing dependence on another's guidance.
terra: Unperceiving humans are compared to livestock and called still further astray, another animal comparison in which failure of guidance is decisive.
terra: Tethered horses are kept ready as organized power, a trained and prepared animal condition set against the unbroken camel of the section.
terra: Hoarders' foreheads, sides, and backs are branded in Hell; جُنُوبُهُمْ at the fire reverses the image of the cautious being led at the side and away.
terra: A moderate journey would have been followed, but the hard distance deterred the reluctant, turning ease, following, and resistance into a road scene.
terra: A structure on a collapsing cliff gives way with its builder into Hell, a concrete image of a seemingly usable footing becoming a fatal descent.
terra: God carries people by land and sea, while the ship's riders discover in the storm that their smooth passage and rescue are not their own achievement.
terra: Noah says to embark in God's name for the ark's course and anchorage, making the vehicle's movement depend on its Lord.
terra: Every creature is under God's grasp at its forelock and the Lord is on a straight path, making the section's unseen holder of the reins almost explicit.
terra: God turns evil and indecency away from Joseph, a moral counterpart to Abraham asking to be led away from shirk.
terra: The wrongdoers have no وَاقٍ against God, defining the limit beyond which no creature can supply its own protective gear or guide.
terra: After revealed knowledge, no protecting ally or وَاقٍ exists against God, marking the limit of creaturely protection.
terra: God subjects ships to run at His command, the maritime form of the animal's bestowed compliance.

luna: The section explicitly cites Ibrahim's prayer وَٱجْنُبْنِى وَبَنِىَّ أَن نَّعْبُدَ ٱلْأَصْنَامَ and explains it through the source-section dictionary verb جنبت الدابة, leading a horse by one's side: being led aside becomes a plea for protection from idolatry. | terra: Abraham asks وَٱجْنُبْنِى وَبَنِىَّ to be kept from idol worship, the exact prayer that the section reads as God leading a mount away from shirk.
terra: Livestock are created with warmth, benefits, and food, supplying the creaturely gift within which the riding function appears.

luna: The section stages a rider carried along a road by a yielding animal. 16:7 says livestock carry loads to a destination people could not reach without great hardship, making the mount's easing of the journey concrete. | terra: Livestock carry loads to a land people could reach only with severe personal hardship, so the compliant animal literally makes a hard road passable.

luna: The section develops a careful horse and a camel that may or may not yield to a rider; 16:8 names horses, mules, and donkeys as animals made for riding, directly extending the same riding scene. | terra: Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding, directly naming the animals and purpose developed by the section.
terra: The direction of the way belongs to God while some ways deviate, and He could have guided everyone; the road and its guidance are under His authority.
terra: Ships plow the sea so people can seek God's bounty and give thanks, another conveyance whose useful motion is assigned to divine provision.
terra: Misleaders bear their own full burdens and part of the burdens of those they mislead, joining following with the weight produced by bad direction.
terra: Every community receives the call to worship God and اجْتَنِبُوا ٱلطَّاغُوتَ, extending Abraham's requested removal into a universal route away from false worship.
terra: Animal skins become dwellings found light on travel days, extending livestock's bestowed usefulness from carrying to portable travel equipment.

luna: The source-section dictionary calls a saddle that does not wound a horse وَاقٍ, from the protection root و ق ي. 16:81 describes clothing and armor that protect people from heat and battle; the same protective function shifts from a mount's back to human bodies. | terra: God provides garments that protect from heat and coats that protect in battle, a Qur'anic counterpart to protective equipment that does not wound its bearer.
terra: The repeated rule that no burden-bearer bears another's burden marks the moral limit of the section's carrying image.
terra: The ban on walking proudly reminds the walker that he cannot split the earth or reach the mountains, checking the illusion that his own stride masters the ground.
terra: The Lord drives ships through the sea so people can seek His bounty, giving divine agency to the motion of the conveyance.
terra: At sea all invoked powers vanish except God, yet after He brings riders safely to land they turn away, exposing failed remembrance of the carrier's true Lord.
luna: The section's rider depends on a creature to bear him along the way. 17:70 says people are carried on land and sea, extending that dependence to human travel generally.

luna: The section's image places the God-fearing person at a distance from the Fire. 19:71 says everyone will approach it; the next ayah distinguishes those God saves, making this approach the boundary that the section's being led aside crosses. | terra: Everyone's coming to Hell is stated as a settled decree; the next ayah's rescue of those with taqwa therefore marks a divinely effected passage through danger.

luna: The section says the most God-fearing are taken aside from the Fire. After 19:71 says everyone will approach it, 19:72 specifies that God saves the God-fearing and leaves the wrongdoers there; this row supplies the selective rescue. | terra: God then saves those who practiced taqwa and leaves wrongdoers kneeling in Hell, directly supporting the claim that the cautious do not secure themselves unaided.
terra: Those with taqwa are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, forming the safe procession opposite criminals driven to Hell in the next ayah.
terra: Criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, the opposite destination for a group under another's direction.
terra: Moses is warned not to let denial of the Hour turn him aside فَتَرْدَىٰ, so diversion from the directed way ends in the same falling root.

luna: The source-section dictionary phrase أعطى البعير names a camel's yielding; 20:50 uses أَعْطَىٰ for God's giving each thing its created form and then guiding it. That puts the mount's fitted, responsive nature under its Creator's gift and guidance. | terra: Moses identifies the Lord as the one who أَعْطَىٰ every thing its created form and then guided it, joining bestowed fitness to bestowed direction.
terra: God makes the earth a cradle and threads roads through it so people may find guidance, another formulation of terrain prepared for passage.
terra: Moses is commanded to make a dry path through the sea and told not to fear pursuit or dread, a divinely opened and protected route through dangerous terrain.
terra: Broad passageways are placed through the earth so people may be guided, turning resistant terrain into traversable routes.
terra: God teaches the making of armor that protects people from violence, a nonlexical parallel to equipment fitted to guard rather than wound.

luna: The section's وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا image keeps the most God-fearing person away from the Fire. 21:101 says those promised the best are kept far from it, giving a direct parallel to that spatial removal. | terra: Those for whom the best has preceded from God are kept far away from Hell, an especially close nonlexical parallel to being made to pass away from the fire.

luna: After 21:101 says the promised people are kept far from the Fire, 21:102 adds that they will not hear even its faintest sound. The neighbour makes the section's distance from the Fire a complete safety. | terra: Those kept far from Hell do not even hear its faintest sound, specifying the completeness of the distance stated in 21:101.
terra: The arrogant person turns his side to lead others away from God's way and is promised the burning punishment, opposing the yielding turn toward a rider.

luna: The section develops the camel as a mount and a road traveled with another's help. 22:27 sends pilgrims toward the Hajj on foot or on lean camels from distant passes, expanding the riding image into a long journey of worship. | terra: Pilgrims come on foot and on every lean camel through every deep mountain pass, placing the riding animal inside an arduous sacred road.
terra: Pilgrims remember God's name over the livestock He provided and feed the needy from them, placing animal provision inside remembrance and giving.
terra: The command فَٱجْتَنِبُوا ٱلرِّجْسَ مِنَ ٱلْأَوْثَانِ uses the root for deliberate distance from idols, the object named in Abraham's prayer.
terra: The one who associates with God is likened to falling from the sky and being snatched or swept far away, the falling end of refusing Abraham's anti-idolatry route.
terra: Livestock are God's provision over which His name is remembered, while humans are told to submit to the one God; animal gift and human yielding meet directly.
terra: Sacrificial animals stand, fall onto their جُنُوب, and are described as subjected by God; animal sides and divine submission meet the section's ج ن ب image.
terra: Their flesh does not reach God but human taqwa does, and their subjection calls for magnifying God for guidance, joining the cautious human, subdued animal, and praise.
terra: God subjects what is on earth and lets ships run by His command, broadening the subdued-mount claim into a governed world of travel.
terra: God has placed no constriction in religion, supporting the section's picture of a divinely fitted rather than needlessly wounding course.
terra: Livestock offer milk, many benefits, and food before the next ayah names them as carriers, framing transport within a larger embodied blessing.

luna: The section emphasizes the rider being carried by another creature. 23:22 says people are carried both upon livestock and ships, extending that relation from the animal road to travel by sea. | terra: People are carried upon livestock and ships, a concise parallel to the section's human whose passage is made by a bearer.
terra: After settling on the ark, Noah is told to praise God for rescue, a vehicle-mounting formula closely parallel to remembering the Lord upon an animal's back.
terra: After the ark's rescue formula, Noah is told to ask his Lord for a blessed landing, placing arrival as well as carriage under divine care.
terra: God charges no soul beyond its capacity, another limit supporting the section's image of a bearer fitted rather than injured by its load.
terra: God creates creatures with distinct modes of movement, including those walking on four legs, grounding the section's attention to animal gait in created form.
terra: Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are described as worst in place and furthest astray from the way, reversing upright safe-leading on a road.
terra: People who will not hear or understand are compared to livestock and said to be further astray from the way, opposing the animal guided along its route.
terra: The servants of the Merciful walk gently upon the earth, turning faithful yielding into a visible manner of placing one's steps.
terra: Servants of the Merciful ask their Lord to turn Hell's punishment away from them, a nonlexical prayer for the same removal.
terra: God could send a sign before which their necks remain bowed, making human submission visible in the same bodily point as the mount turning toward its rider.
terra: When apparently trapped on the journey, Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him, placing confidence in the route's divine guide.
terra: The false gods and the erring are toppled headlong into Hell, giving misdirection the falling end anticipated by the section.
terra: God saves those who believed and had taqwa from the destruction of Salih's opponents, making rescue the divine answer to caution.
terra: Setting out toward Midian, Moses hopes his Lord will guide him to the right way, a travel prayer for direction.
terra: Disbelievers invite others to follow their way and promise to carry their sins, but the ayah denies that they can bear any of them.
terra: They will bear their own burdens and burdens added to them, exposing the deceptive offer of an easy follower's road in the preceding ayah.
terra: Ship riders call sincerely on God in danger but associate partners after He saves them, reversing the remembrance required upon mounting.
terra: God sends winds so ships may sail by His command and people may seek His bounty and give thanks, linking motion to gift and gratitude.
terra: Turning one's cheek away and walking exultantly oppose the camel that turns its head toward its rider and the person whose gait is disciplined.
terra: The command وَٱقْصِدْ فِى مَشْيِكَ calls for a measured gait, a human counterpart to the controlled pace of the section's horse.
terra: Ships travel through the sea by God's blessing so He may show His signs, explicitly treating conveyance as grace to the patient and grateful.
terra: A heavily laden soul cannot have its load carried even by close kin, sharpening the boundary between bodily transport and accountable burden.
terra: God could fix people in their places so they could neither proceed nor return, showing that even the ability to move along a route is bestowed.

luna: The section quotes 36:71's claim that people own the livestock, then 36:72 says God subdued them for riding. This verse's own claim of ownership is bounded by the following verse's reminder that their usefulness depends on God's subduing. | terra: God says He made livestock for people and they became their owners, directly supplying the ownership side of the section's mount scene.

luna: The section's dictionary branch says the camel's أعطى means yielding to its rider; 36:72 says God subdued the animals for people and made some their mounts. The verse makes the animal's compliance a granted condition of riding. | terra: وَذَلَّلْنَاهَا describes God's subduing livestock so that some become mounts, locating the animal's docility in divine action.
terra: The subdued animals also yield benefits and drink, and the question about gratitude frames that usefulness as a gift.
terra: Wrongdoers are commanded to be guided to the path of Hell, the terrible reverse of being led alongside and away from the fire.
terra: The saved person sees his former companion in the midst of Hell, locating the near-ruin named in the following ayah.
terra: A saved speaker tells his former companion that he nearly أَن تُرْدِينِ, casting the section's fall as ruin toward Hell.
terra: He credits his Lord's favor for not being brought among the condemned, making rescue from the threatened fall a gift.
terra: The poised, swift horses presented to Solomon put both trained stillness and fleet movement into one Qur'anic mount scene.
terra: Solomon's response to the horses binds the mount display to remembrance of his Lord, though the exact force of his statement about love is disputed.
terra: The recalled horses bring legs and necks into view; the precise action is disputed, but these are the same bodily points through which the section depicts pace and response.
terra: No burden-bearer bears another's burden before return to the Lord, setting individual return against reliance on another carrier.
terra: Those who اجْتَنَبُوا ٱلطَّاغُوتَ from worship and turn to God receive good news, joining avoidance with a changed direction.
terra: A chest opened to submission and light is set against hearts hardened toward God's remembrance, defining the human resistance opposite the softened mount.
terra: Skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance; human yielding is bodily felt and is then named as God's guidance.
terra: The condemned person tries to shield the face from terrible punishment, a bodily but futile form of protection opposite divine safe-leading.

luna: The section pictures the God-fearing being led to safety by another. 39:61 says God delivers those who were mindful to their place of triumph, a direct statement of rescue for the God-fearing. | terra: God saves those who had taqwa in their place of attainment so that evil does not touch them, naming divine rescue as the outcome of caution.

luna: The section's God-fearing person is taken aside from Hell; 39:71 drives disbelievers toward it. The same externally directed movement ends in the opposite destination. | terra: Disbelievers are driven in companies to Hell, showing an imposed journey whose destination reverses the protective leading in the section.

luna: After 39:71's disbelievers are driven to Hell, 39:72 opens its gates and names their destination as a lasting abode. That continuation completes the opposite route to the section's person being led away from the Fire.

luna: The section pictures the most God-fearing person being led away from the Fire by another. 39:73 says those who feared their Lord are driven in groups to Paradise; the passive leading preserves the dependence on a guide while reversing the destination. | terra: Those with taqwa are driven in companies to the Garden, a positive procession in which the cautious are conveyed to safety.
terra: The angels ask God to protect believers from evil consequences and declare that whoever He protects that Day has received mercy.
terra: On the day people turn their backs fleeing, no protector from God exists, and one He lets stray has no guide; protection and direction both reach their boundary.
terra: God protects Pharaoh's believing man from the evils of the plot, showing وَقَى as an enacted rescue rather than merely personal caution.

luna: The section treats animal docility and carriage as divine provision. 40:79 says God made livestock so that people ride some and eat others, matching the mount as a bestowed use. | terra: God makes livestock so that people ride some and eat from others, explicitly presenting the ride as His provision.

luna: The section describes the mount carrying its rider as a benefit not produced by the rider. 40:80 adds that people reach needs in their hearts through livestock and are carried on them and on ships, specifying the practical value of being carried. | terra: Livestock meet needs held in people's breasts, and people are carried on them as on ships; the rider's attainment depends on another bearer.
terra: God saves the believers who had taqwa from the punishing wind, another concrete event in which the cautious are delivered by Him.
terra: God's enemies are gathered toward the Fire and marshaled together, an imposed procession opposite being conducted away from it.
terra: The false assumption about God أَرْدَىٰ its holders, using the section's falling-ruin root for the belief that brings them to loss.
terra: Ships like landmarks on the sea are counted among God's signs, identifying the conveyances whose motion He can stop in the next ayah.
terra: God can still the wind and leave ships motionless on the sea, exposing the limit of the rider's power over a subjected conveyance.
terra: The believers are those who avoid major sins and indecencies, using the same root family for a practiced distance from harm.
terra: God makes the earth a resting place and lays paths in it so people may find direction, immediately before the surah's mounting scene.

luna: The section's image is of a person riding a made-subservient animal. 43:12 names ships and riding animals among what God created; it sets up the next verse's mounting, gratitude, and acknowledgement of dependence. | terra: God makes both ships and livestock into conveyances people ride; the mount belongs to a created and divinely fitted order.

luna: The section says the docility of a mount is a blessing rather than the rider's achievement. In 43:13 the rider is to remember God's favor and say سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا and مَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ, naming both the gift and human inability. | terra: On settling upon their backs, riders must remember their Lord's blessing and say that He subjected the mount because they could not master it themselves.

luna: The section frames the mount as a reminder of its Lord. 43:14 follows the riding recollection of 43:13 with the rider's return to the Lord, giving the journey an eschatological direction. | terra: The riding formula ends by naming return to the Lord, giving the section's road and carried rider their final destination.
terra: The blessed are described as having been protected from the punishment of the Blaze, another direct divine enactment of the section's protective stance.

luna: The section recalls the rider thanking God for a mount made serviceable by Him. 45:12 applies that dependence to the sea: ships run by God's command so people may seek His bounty and give thanks, extending the same travel-and-gratitude relation beyond the road. | terra: God subjects the sea so ships may sail by His command and people may seek His bounty and be grateful.
terra: God increases the guided in guidance and gives them their taqwa, supporting the section's sense that even the traveler's caution is bestowed.
terra: Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, making externally directed passage into the judgment scene explicit.

luna: The source-section root و ق ي joins careful avoidance to protection; 52:18 says their Lord protected them from Hell's punishment. It gives the divine protection behind the section's image of being led away from the Fire. | terra: The people of the Garden rejoice because their Lord وَوَقَاهُمْ from the punishment of Hell, using the protection root with God as protector.
terra: The saved confess that God favored them and وَوَقَانَا from the scorching torment, joining grace, protection, and deliverance from fire.
terra: Those who avoid major sins and indecencies enact the self-directed avoidance that the section distinguishes from being led away by God.

luna: The source-section dictionary phrase أعطى البعير uses أعطى for a camel's yielding. 53:34 describes a person who gives a little and then stops, making the same giving form a specific human counterpoint to the mount's yielding. | terra: The person gives only a little and then withholds, a human refusal that contrasts with the fully yielding sense attached to أَعْطَى in the section.
terra: The scripture's rule that no bearer bears another's burden supplies another explicit boundary for the mount-and-load image.
terra: People rush toward the summoner while the disbelievers call it a difficult day, joining compelled movement with the Qur'anic ʿusr outcome.
terra: Criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire, the coercive and ruinous opposite of being led safely beside it.
terra: Criminals are seized by forelocks and feet, turning the section's guided animal anatomy into coercive capture at judgment.
terra: Believers are called to let their hearts humble to remembrance rather than become hardened, developing the human yielding behind the softened-animal comparison.
terra: The believers had urged neither horses nor riding camels toward the recovered property; control of the outcome is instead expressly assigned to God.
terra: Those protected from the stinginess of their own souls succeed, connecting divine و ق ي protection specifically with the giver's opposite, inner avarice.
terra: The donkey carrying books bears a load without receiving its meaning, setting a limit on what faithful carrying and following amount to.
terra: The command to fear God and spend is followed by the promise that whoever is protected from the soul's stinginess succeeds.
terra: For whoever has taqwa, God makes a way out, turning cautious conduct into an exit supplied from beyond the traveler.
terra: Whoever has taqwa is promised that God will make his affair ease, directly reuniting the cautious step with divinely supplied yusr.

luna: The section sets the untrained camel's resistance against the mount made easy to follow. 65:7 promises that God will bring ease after difficulty, expressing the same change of condition in a human provision context. | terra: God promises to make yusr after ʿusr, presenting hard passage as a condition He can replace with ease.

luna: The source-section root و ق ي includes avoiding harm, and 92:17 depicts the God-fearing being moved aside from the Fire. 66:6 commands believers to protect themselves and their families from it, contrasting active guarding with the section's passive rescue. | terra: قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا commands active guarding from a fire, the imperative boundary beside 92:17's passive promise of being kept from it.

luna: The section develops a horse that must read the ground and a mount made easy to follow; 67:15 calls the earth ذَلُولًا and tells people to walk its slopes. It moves the image of a tractable surface from the animal to the ground beneath the traveler. | terra: God makes the earth ذَلُولًا and tells people to walk its slopes, transferring animal tractability to terrain made traversable by Him.
terra: The one walking fallen upon his face is set against one walking upright on a straight path, directly testing gait, guidance, and the road's outcome.

luna: The section links 92:11's falling to the failure of wealth to help its owner. In 69:28 the speaker says his wealth did not avail him, a direct eschatological counterpart that clarifies the limit of worldly possession at the fall.
luna: After 69:28 says wealth did not avail, 69:29 says the speaker's authority has vanished. It completes the section's claim that property cannot help at the moment of falling.
terra: God makes the earth an expanse for people, preparing the terrain rather than leaving it intrinsically resistant.
terra: The purpose is that people travel broad paths through it, a direct road consequence of the earth's divine preparation.
terra: The Day is called a difficult day, giving eschatological content to the ʿusr toward which the resistant person is eased.

luna: The source-section dictionary calls an unbroken camel العسير; 74:10 says the Day is غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ for disbelievers. The difficulty shifts from an animal's untrained movement to the final day, extending the root's contrast without equating the scenes. | terra: That difficult Day is expressly not easy for disbelievers, placing yusr and its negation around the denier's destination.
terra: Those fleeing the reminder are likened to startled donkeys, a vivid animal reversal of the calm, quickly following mount.
terra: The donkeys flee from a lion, specifying the uncontrolled fear that drives the contrary animal gait in 74:50.
terra: After denying and turning away, the person goes swaggering to his people, giving rejection the opposite gait from a soft, quickly following mount.
terra: فَوَقَاهُمُ ٱللَّهُ makes God the one who protects the generous and fearful from that Day and meets them with radiance and joy.
terra: ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ says God eases the human being's way, directly combining divine facilitation with a path.
terra: Valuable pregnant camels are abandoned at the Hour, overturning ordinary ownership and reliance on the useful animal.
terra: God creates and proportions, supplying the creaturely fitness presupposed by an animal able to bear and move well.
terra: God determines and guides, completing 87:2's fitted creature with direction rather than leaving movement self-generated.

luna: The source-section root ي س ر describes an animal that is easy to follow and light in its legs. 87:8 says God will ease the addressee toward ease, preserving the section's sense that ease is made possible by another. | terra: وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى closely repeats the divine promise to ease a person toward ease, the verbal motion beneath the tractable mount.

luna: The section's source dictionaries develop the yielding and untrained camel; 88:17 asks people to look at the camels and how they were created. It directs attention to the created animal whose behavior the section reads closely. | terra: The command to look at how the camel was created invites attention to precisely the creaturely capacities the section draws out.
terra: The person has not undertaken the steep pass, making moral giving an ascent through resisting terrain rather than an abstract choice.
terra: The question about what the steep pass is holds the road image open for the acts of release and giving that follow.
terra: Freeing a neck is the first meaning assigned to the steep pass, so moral release becomes the act by which difficult terrain is crossed.
terra: Feeding on a day of hunger continues the definition of the steep pass through costly giving.
terra: The orphan of near relation specifies one recipient of the giving that constitutes ascent over the pass.
terra: The destitute person in misery completes the concrete giving by which the steep pass is traversed.
terra: The soul is inspired with both its rebellion and its taqwa, treating protective discernment as something given to it.
terra: The Lord promises to give until the addressee is satisfied, reversing the direction of human أَعْطَى and locating final sufficiency in the divine giver.

luna: The source-section roots ي س ر and ع س ر distinguish the easy-following mount from the untrained camel; 94:5 states that with hardship comes ease, putting that contrast into a promise about hardship. | terra: The assurance that with ʿusr comes yusr states the coexistence that the section distributes between the resistant and compliant journeys.

luna: The section treats the rider's apparent control as dependence on the One who tamed the mount and leads the saved. 96:6 says the human being transgresses; 96:7 identifies the accompanying illusion of self-sufficiency, a contrary stance to the section's dependence.

luna: The section says a rider's ease and the saved person's safety come from a giver beyond themselves. 96:7 describes a person who sees himself as self-sufficient, the opposite stance that makes dependence on a gift visible.

luna: If the oath's العاديات are read as charging horses, 100:1 gives the fast, panting gait opposite the source-section dictionary's horse that moves cautiously to spare a painful hoof. The horse reading is traditional, so this is a specific but interpretive parallel. | terra: The panting chargers run at full exertion, a sharp counterpart to the hoof-sore horse that fears placing its foot.

luna: On the same horse reading of 100:1, 100:2 continues the rush with sparks struck in the charge; this reverses the source-section's hoof-sensitive horse that avoids painful steps. terra: The charging animals raise dust, making the ground's response to their fast footfall visible within the continued horse scene.
terra: The chargers penetrate into the midst of the gathering, completing the horse sequence with fast, directed arrival rather than hesitant footing.

terra: The hoarder will be cast into the Crusher, turning trust in wealth into an externally imposed plunge.
